raw_plan.interpretation: I interpret this as one acquisition email for an unknown-relationship, product-aware prospect. Following the current dossier, the selected audience is narrowed to freelancers delivering a client project; the email earns a product evaluation rather than assuming readiness to buy.

intent.desired_action: Look inside the Your Plans on Paper productivity planner and decide whether its planning structure fits one client project.

raw_plan.reader: A freelancer considering a paper system for organising daily work toward a substantial client-project goal over a focused 16-week period.
raw_plan.reader_segment: A goal-driven professional starting a focused 16-week push and wanting planning away from screens
raw_plan.reader_scope: Freelancers delivering a client project within the selected audience; do not generalise the fit to all goal-driven professionals.
raw_plan.promise: A freelancer can give one client project a defined place on paper, moving from a 16-week goal to smaller breakdowns and monthly, weekly and daily planning.
raw_plan.orientation: A paper productivity planner for an individual professional organising daily work toward a substantial goal over a focused 16-week period.
raw_plan.arc: In one self-contained email, move from a concrete client-project use case to the planner's bounded mechanism, then invite the reader to inspect the pages and judge the fit.
raw_plan.sequence_rationale: Because the contract requires exactly one email and the reader is product-aware, the email should lead directly with the checkable 16-week planning mechanism rather than explain the category or invent a failing workflow. The look-inside action lets the reader make a smaller, relevant evaluation before any purchase decision. The researched rolling-calendar problem does not lead because the documented fit is only partial.

emails.selection_reason: The bounded 16-week format and goal breakdowns map directly to a freelancer organising one substantial client project, while the product page offers a documented look-inside step before purchase.

value_case.reader_benefit: If a client project suits a 16-week planning cycle, the freelancer can break its goal down and organise the work across monthly, weekly and daily paper pages.
value_case.mechanism: The planner provides 16 weeks of undated pages, goal breakdowns, and monthly, weekly and daily planning pages.
decision_conditions: The proposition applies when the client project can usefully be organised within a focused 16-week cycle.
The pages are undated; the evidence does not specify the planner's total page count.

emails.target_audience: Freelancers delivering a client project who want a focused 16-week paper planning system.
emails.job: Earn a relevant evaluation by getting the reader to inspect whether the planner's page structure fits one client project.
emails.single_idea: Give one client project a defined 16-week place on paper, with goal breakdowns connected to monthly, weekly and daily planning.
emails.mechanism: Start with the project's goal, break it down across 16 undated weeks, and use the monthly, weekly and daily pages to organise the work on paper.

alternative_arguments.selection_reason: This is a distinct, supported reason to evaluate the planner for a client project: its reflections and accountability tools make progress review part of the planning cycle, rather than focusing only on scheduling layers.

value_case.reader_benefit: A freelancer can use the planner's tracking tools and reflections to record and review progress during a client-project push.
value_case.mechanism: The productivity planner includes accountability tracking tools and reflections intended for tracking progress.
decision_conditions: The individual accountability tools and the frequency or structure of reflections are not described.
No measured improvement in progress is established.

alternative_arguments.single_idea: Build progress review into a client project's paper plan through accountability tools and reflections.
alternative_arguments.mechanism: Use the included accountability tracking tools during the project and the reflection sections to record progress.
alternative_arguments.belief_shift: Before: a paper planner may appear useful only for laying out tasks. After: this planner also includes documented mechanisms for tracking and reflecting on project progress.
must_not_say: Do not promise that the tools improve accountability, productivity, delivery speed or project outcomes.
Do not invent the form, frequency or contents of the accountability tools or reflections.

alternative_arguments.next_step_decision: Decide whether built-in tracking and reflection are relevant enough to continue evaluating the planner for a client project.
alternative_arguments.next_step_value: The official productivity-planner page documents that accountability tracking tools and reflections are included.
alternative_arguments.next_step_limit: The page does not establish the exact design or frequency of these tools, or any resulting improvement in project delivery.
alternative_arguments.subject_strategy: Create curiosity around reviewing progress during a client-project push, without promising better performance or implying the reader has an accountability problem.

data.preview_text: See how goal breakdowns connect with monthly, weekly and daily paper planning.
data.body:
When one client project suits a focused 16-week cycle, give it a place of its own—away from the screen and open on your desk.

Your Plans on Paper is Papier’s softback spiral productivity planner, with 16 weeks of undated pages. Start with its goal breakdowns, then organise the work across the planning pages.

Monthly for the wider view. Weekly for what comes next. Daily for what belongs on today’s page. One project, three useful distances.

Flick through the planner on the product page to inspect the monthly, weekly and daily layouts, then decide whether its 16-week structure fits the way you would organise your client project.
